grade.first_issue: In the k=2 case, the proof chooses P as the foot of the altitude from A without ensuring that this foot lies in the interior of BC, as required. This is repaired directly by choosing an appropriate vertex—for example, a largest-angle vertex—whose altitude is internal when the triangle does not already contain a right angle.
grade.summary: The characterization is correct, and both directions are essentially proved. The sufficiency strategy correctly produces a small angle, converts it into the multiple (k−1)θ, and peels multiples down to θ. The necessity argument establishes the invariant that a triangle with no positive-integer multiple of θ always has at least one similarly safe child. The proof has only directly repairable local defects, chiefly the unqualified altitude choice, a missing explicit justification that a safe starting triangle exists, and one harmless sign reversal in the third case of the invariant calculation.
strengths: Correct final set θ=180°/k for integers k≥2.
The small-angle construction is explicitly checked for positivity and produces the crucial angle (k−1)θ.
The peeling argument correctly handles every positive multiple of θ.
The necessity proof exhausts all four ways both children could acquire a multiple of θ and thereby gives Shan-Yu a valid invariant strategy.

errors.description: For θ=90°, the perpendicular from an arbitrarily labeled vertex A need not meet the interior of BC. The proof should specify an internal altitude, obtainable by choosing a suitable vertex.
The necessity proof asserts without construction that Shan-Yu can initially choose three nonmultiples of θ summing to 180°. This is easy to supply, for instance with (θ/2, θ/2, 180°−θ).
In the third of the four necessity cases, nθ−C=mθ implies C=(n−m)θ, not C=(m−n)θ. Since C>0, the corrected equality still gives the claimed contradiction.
